chapter: Manhattan School of Music and Eddie Durham
title: Manhattan School of Music and Phil Schaap's West End Cafe
summary: Entering MSM in 1976, studying with Joe Allard, and Phil Schaap's seven-night jazz scene at the West End.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Okay. Let me get back to your bio a bit. Was it, the Benny Goodman association, did it take some getting used to with Benny?

Well what happened was I went to Manhattan School of Music in 1976. Music theory major, piano minor. And eventually switched to saxophone major, which means that I got to study with Joe Allard, who was a great teacher, a guy named Dave Tofani, but at the same time, Manhattan School of Music is in the old Juilliard building. It’s up at 122nd Street and Claremont Avenue in Manhattan. And just down the street from where I was living was a club called the West End that was run by Phil Schaap. And this is a major moment. I mean I hope somebody, you know, writes a monograph or a thesis on what Phil Schaap did at the West End Café in the 1970s. Because what he did was, people like, well I won’t name names, but there were great musicians from the Fletcher Henderson, Count Basie, Jay McShann bands, who were working as bank guards or working as literally messengers on Wall Street, just you know, walking around like the bag I had around their neck and delivering stock things. I mean they were not making a living in music and they were struggling. So what Phil did was Phil put together seven nights a week of jazz at the West End. Jo Jones one day. Harold Ashby the next night. Sammy Price the next night. Eddie Durham, Francis Williams, Ram Ramirez, guys who played with Louis Armstrong you probably never heard of. George James. Drummers like Percy Brice and, and Sonny Greer. I got to work with Sonny Greer there. And what Phil — I mean not only was it musically fascinating because my God there’s like these giants of a past era, they’re playing right there every night, you can hang out and listen. But also he gave them a social life. In other words for a musician who had played with Count Basie or Duke Ellington or Erskine Hawkins or one of those great bands, to know that Thursday night I’m putting on my suit, I’m getting my horn out, I’m going to play, and this crazy guy, this crazy Phil Schaap guy who knows everything that there ever was about jazz, he’s going to be there and he’s going to know that I played the solo on this alternate take of “King Porter Stomp.” You know that meant so much to these people. It was a profound thing. And so I lived around the corner. The first two years, I mean Manhattan School of Music had no dormitories. So we lived in apartments mostly owned by old ladies who were known to the school that they could tell your parents oh he’s going to be rooming with Mrs. Ashe and she’s had students for thirty years and she’s very safe and all this kind of stuff. So I lived at an apartment at 112th and Riverside Drive that was just around the corner from the West End. And you know I was so desp — not desperate, I was desperate to sit in and to play, and they see a young guy come in with a saxophone oh my God it’s going to be another these guys that doesn’t know the songs.
